blocks.text: The second proof is drawn from those passages of Scripture in which the hasida is treated. For in them whatever is attributed to the hasida fits the stork best. To make this plain to the reader, it is worth running through and examining all of them.

I. Moses counts the hasida among the unclean birds and forbids the Jews to eat it. This suits the stork exceedingly well, for it feeds on serpents and venomous animals, and in the nest it feeds its young on no other food. Juvenal, Satire 14:
— — the stork feeds its young on the serpent, and on the lizard found in the trackless fields.

Hence it was highly prized in Thessaly. Aristotle in the Marvels: Περὶ Θετταλίαν μνημονεύουσιν ὄφεις ζωογονηθῆναι τοσούτους, ὥστε. εἰ μὴ ὑπὸ τῶν πελαργῶν ἀνῃροῦντο, ἐκχωρῆσαι ἂν αὐτούς· [Peri Thettalian mnēmoneuousin opheis zōogonēthēnai tosoutous, hōste ei mē hypo tōn pelargōn anērounto, ekchōrēsai an autous] They say that around Thessaly so many serpents are bred that, were they not destroyed by the storks, the region would have to be abandoned. Plutarch in Isis: Θεσσαλοὶ δὲ πελαργοὺς (ἐτίμησαν), ὅτι, πολλοὺς ὄφεις τῆς γῆς ἀναδιδούσης, ἐπιφανέντες ἐξώλεσαν ἅπαντας· [Thessaloi de pelargous (etimēsan), hoti, pollous opheis tēs gēs anadidousēs, epiphanentes exōlesan hapantas] The Thessalians held storks in honour, because, when their land had produced many serpents, [III, 88] they destroyed them all by their arrival. Pliny, book 10, chapter 23: So great is the honour paid them for destroying serpents that in Thessaly it was a capital crime to have killed one. Solinus on Thessaly: Where there is an enormous quantity of serpents; by hunting them for food (the storks) remove a great deal of harm from the Thessalian districts. So too Belon on Egypt: The Egyptians rightly [col. 329] love storks, both because of the frogs, which are born there in excessive abundance and which they consume, and because they even swallow serpents whole. Accordingly the Muslims still dispute today whether it is lawful to eat اللغلق [al-laghlaq] alleklek, that is, the stork. Some indeed permit it, كالكركي [ka-l-kurkī] like the crane: but most forbid it, بانه ياكل الحيات [bi-annahu yaʾkul al-ḥayyāt] because it eats serpents. Thus from the rule by which all water birds are permitted this bird alone is excepted, with a further reason added, that دف في طيرانه كما تفعل الجوارح [daffa fī ṭayarānihi kamā tafʿal al-jawāriḥ] it moves its wings in flight as if beating with them, as birds of prey do, all of which are forbidden. The theologians of that impure sect explain this at greater length in Damir. That the leklek is the stork, not the crane, as many explain it in Avicenna, is shown both by the description itself and by this statement of Abenbitar: فالرغوس هو اللغلق [fālarghūs huwa al-laghlaq] Πελαργὸς [Pelargos] is alleklek. It is also written with Gain, اللغلغ [al-laghlagh] allegleg, although in the Alcamus some would have لقلق [laqlaq] leklek and لغلغ [laghlagh] legleg be different birds; but wrongly, since no description anywhere exists of a bird لغلغ [laghlagh] legleg distinct from the stork. And Damir begins his treatise On the stork thus: اللغلق طاير طويل العنق وربما قالوا اللغلغ [al-laghlaq ṭāʾir ṭawīl al-ʿunuq wa-rubbamā qālū al-laghlagh] Alleklek, a long-necked bird, which they sometimes call allegleg. From both is compounded the Turkish name of the stork, leglek, in Gesner, for which one should read leklek or legleg. And it is wrongly called Turkish, since it is purely Arabic. The Turkish word, however, is tuigon, as Busbecq asserts in his Letters On the Turkish embassy ^{(2)}.
